data.content: You and four friends pool in ₹10,000 each to start a chai tapri near your college. Five people, ₹50,000 total. Each of you owns 20% of the business. If the tapri earns ₹1 lakh profit, you each pocket ₹20,000. If it shuts down tomorrow, you each lose ₹10,000.
That 20% slice you hold? That's literally what a stock is. Ownership of a business, split into pieces.

data.alt: Five friends splitting ownership of a chai tapri equally
data.prompt: Five Indian teens standing around a colorful chai tapri stall, each holding a small flag showing 20%. Green (#2ECC71) color palette, bold flat illustration style, fun and vibrant, filling the entire frame.

data.content: Now scale that up massively. Instead of a chai tapri, picture Reliance Industries -- the company behind your Jio SIM, the Reliance Fresh store near your house, and half the petrol pumps you see on any highway. Instead of 5 friends, millions of investors each own a tiny slice. Maybe 0.0001%.
Each of those tiny slices has a name. It's called a share (or a stock). You buy one, you own a piece of that giant company. For real.

data.definition: A unit of ownership in a company. When you buy one share of TCS, you literally own a (very tiny) piece of Tata Consultancy Services.

data.text: Wait, so if I buy one share of Reliance, I actually own a piece of Mukesh Ambani's company? Like, for real for real?
Haan yaar, for real! A tiny piece, obviously. You won't get invited to board meetings with one share. But legally? You are a part-owner of Reliance. Pretty sick, right?

data.question: If you buy one share of Reliance Industries, what do you become?

options.text: A lender who is owed money by Reliance
A part-owner of Reliance Industries
An employee of Reliance Industries

data.content: So why would a massive company like Infosys want millions of strangers owning pieces of it? Simple answer: money. When a company wants to grow -- build new offices, hire thousands of engineers, expand to new countries -- it needs serious cash.

It can borrow that cash (take a loan). Or it can sell ownership slices (issue shares). Selling shares means no repayment, no interest. In exchange, shareholders get a vote in how the company is run and a cut of the profits.

data.definition: The first time a company sells its shares to the public. Think of it as the company's 'grand opening' on the stock market. Zomato's IPO was in July 2021.

data.content: Zomato's IPO in July 2021 was one of India's most hyped launches ever. The issue price was ₹76 per share. Within hours of listing, it hit ₹116 -- a 52% jump in a single day. Early investors made ₹40 per share by literally doing nothing except applying on time.

data.question: Why does a company like Infosys issue shares through an IPO?

options.text: To give free money to the public
To raise funds for growth without taking loans
Because SEBI forces every company to sell shares
To reduce the number of employees

data.alt: Diagram showing how a company's ownership is divided into thousands of shares
data.prompt: A large pie chart divided into many equal slices representing company ownership. One slice is highlighted in bright green (#2ECC71) and labeled 'Your share'. Below the pie: '10,000 total shares x Rs 100/share = Rs 10,00,000 total value'. Bold flat style, clean minimal design, green color palette.

data.content: Here's the crucial difference you need to nail down. Buying a stock is NOT giving a loan. When you lend money, the borrower has to pay you back no matter what. Stocks don't work like that.

If the company does well, your share becomes worth more and you might get dividends (a cut of the profits). If the company tanks? Your share drops in value. Zero guarantees. That's the trade-off for potentially much higher returns.

data.definition: A portion of a company's profit paid out to shareholders. Like a thank-you bonus for owning the stock. Not all companies pay dividends; many reinvest profits into growth instead.

data.question: Zomato's IPO in 2021 was priced at ₹76 per share. What happened on listing day?

options.text: It fell to ₹50, losing investors money
It stayed exactly at ₹76
It jumped to ₹116, a 52% gain
Trading was halted due to low demand

data.content: Buying a stock = owning a piece of a real business. Next time you order on Zomato, remember -- someone out there literally owns a slice of that app. Could be your neighbour. Could be you.

Let's talk numbers. TCS (Tata Consultancy Services) is India's most valuable company, worth over ₹13 lakh crore. It has over 34 crore shares out there. Owning 1 share means you own roughly 0.000000003% of TCS.
Sounds pointless? Not when prices move. If TCS goes from ₹3,800 to ₹4,200, your one share just made you ₹400. Own 1,000 shares? That's ₹4 lakh of profit. While you were attending class.

data.alt: TCS company building with its massive market cap value displayed
data.prompt: A bold flat illustration of a large modern office building labeled 'TCS' with a giant green (#2ECC71) banner reading 'Market Cap: Rs 13 Lakh Crore'. Small figures of people below for scale. Green color palette, clean composition filling the frame.

data.definition: The total value of all a company's shares combined. Formula: Share Price x Total Shares. TCS at ₹3,800/share x 340 crore shares = roughly ₹13 lakh crore market cap.

data.question: How is a company's market capitalisation calculated?

options.text: Annual revenue minus expenses
Share price multiplied by total number of shares
Total dividend payments over 10 years

data.content: So the stock market is basically a giant bazaar where people buy and sell these ownership slices. The price of each slice changes every second based on how many people want to buy vs sell, the company's earnings, the news cycle, and honestly sometimes just vibes. We'll unpack all of it. But first, let's meet the two places where all this buying and selling actually happens in India.

Key mindset shift: when you own a stock, you own part of a real business with real employees, real customers, and real profits. It's not a lottery ticket. It's a tiny ownership certificate. That framing will completely change how you think about investing.

data.alt: A bustling marketplace where people trade ownership slices of companies
data.prompt: A vibrant flat illustration of a marketplace bazaar where stalls display company logos (Reliance, Infosys, Tata) instead of goods. Indian teens browsing the stalls. Green (#2ECC71) palette, bold shapes, lively composition filling the space.

exercises.scenario: Priya and her two brothers want to open a restaurant. They need ₹3,00,000. Priya puts in ₹1,50,000, and each brother puts in ₹75,000. A year later, the restaurant earns ₹60,000 in profit.
exercises.prompt: How much profit should Priya receive?

options.text: ₹20,000, split equally between three people
₹30,000, she owns 50%, so she gets 50% of profit
₹60,000, she put in the most money so she gets everything
₹0, profits should be reinvested in the business

exercises.explanation: Priya owns 50% of the business (₹1,50,000 out of ₹3,00,000). So she gets 50% of the ₹60,000 profit = ₹30,000. Each brother owns 25% and gets ₹15,000 each. This is exactly how stock ownership works, your share of profits matches your share of ownership.

exercises.prompt: A company issues an IPO to raise funds. What does IPO stand for?

options.text: International Profit Organisation
Initial Public Offering
Investor Portfolio Option
Indexed Price Outcome

exercises.explanation: IPO = Initial Public Offering. It's the first time a private company sells shares to the general public. After the IPO, the shares trade freely on the stock exchange every day.

exercises.prompt: When you buy a stock, the company is obligated to return your money if you need it back.
exercises.explanation: Stocks are NOT loans. The company has no obligation to return your money. You get your money back only by selling your shares to someone else on the stock exchange, and only at whatever the market price is at that time. This is why stocks carry risk.

exercises.prompt: If TCS has 340 crore total shares and is currently trading at ₹3,800 per share, what is TCS's market cap approximately?

options.text: ₹3,800 crore
₹13 lakh crore
₹340 crore
₹1 lakh crore

exercises.explanation: Market Cap = Share Price × Total Shares = ₹3,800 × 340 crore = ₹12,92,000 crore ≈ ₹13 lakh crore. This is why TCS is called India's most valuable company, its total ownership value exceeds that of any other Indian company.

exercises.prompt: Which of the following are true about owning a stock? (Select all that apply)

options.text: You become a part-owner of the company
You may receive dividends if the company shares profits
The company must repay you with interest
Your investment can go down in value

exercises.explanation: Stocks give you ownership and potential dividends, but no repayment guarantee. Unlike a fixed deposit or bond, your stock can lose value. That's the trade-off for the potentially higher returns.

data.content: You know how every city has that one famous market? Chandni Chowk in Delhi, Crawford Market in Mumbai, T. Nagar in Chennai. A stock exchange is basically that -- a marketplace. Except instead of vegetables and clothes, people here buy and sell ownership of companies.
India has two main exchanges: the BSE and the NSE. They both do the same job, but they've got very different backstories.

data.alt: Two grand market buildings side by side representing BSE and NSE
data.prompt: Two grand buildings side by side. Left building is old and ornate labeled 'BSE - Est. 1875', right building is modern and sleek labeled 'NSE - Est. 1992'. Indian flag on top of each. Green (#2ECC71) color palette, bold flat illustration style, filling the frame.

data.content: Picture this: it's 1875, India is under British rule, and a group of stockbrokers are meeting under a banyan tree on a street in Mumbai to trade shares. That street is now called Dalal Street. And that informal gathering became the Bombay Stock Exchange -- Asia's oldest stock exchange. Today, BSE lists over 5,000 companies and sits in the iconic Phiroze Jeejeebhoy Towers.

data.definition: Founded in 1875, Asia's oldest stock exchange. Located on Dalal Street, Mumbai. Home to the Sensex index (30 stocks). Lists 5,000+ companies.

data.content: Dalal Street literally means 'Broker's Street' in Hindi. When Indians say 'D-Street is rallying,' it's the same energy as Americans saying 'Wall Street is up.' Same vibe, desi version.

data.question: Which stock exchange is Asia's oldest, founded in 1875?

options.text: NSE (National Stock Exchange)
BSE (Bombay Stock Exchange)
Shanghai Stock Exchange

data.content: Fast forward to 1992. BSE had dominated Indian markets for over a century, but it was still old-school -- noisy trading floors, handwritten slips, zero transparency. The government set up the National Stock Exchange to modernize everything. NSE brought fully electronic trading to India. No more shouting. Just computers. Fast ones.

Today NSE handles way more daily trading volume than BSE and is the world's largest exchange for derivatives (advanced financial contracts like futures and options -- don't worry, those come in later chapters) by number of contracts.

data.definition: Founded in 1992. India's largest exchange by trading volume. Home to the Nifty 50 index. Introduced fully electronic trading in India. World's largest exchange for derivatives (advanced contracts based on stocks) by contract volume.

data.text: So if both exchanges exist, which one do people actually use? Do you have to pick one like picking between Zomato and Swiggy?
Nah, most big companies like Infosys are listed on both! But most of us end up trading on NSE because it has more liquidity -- basically your orders get filled faster there.

data.alt: Side-by-side comparison cards of BSE and NSE with key facts
data.prompt: Two info cards side by side. Left card: BSE with bull icon, 'Founded 1875', 'Sensex (30 stocks)', '5000+ listed companies', 'Asia's oldest'. Right card: NSE with lightning bolt, 'Founded 1992', 'Nifty 50', '2000+ listed', 'World #1 derivatives'. Green (#2ECC71) accents, bold flat design, clean layout.

data.definition: How easy it is to buy or sell something quickly without the price moving too much. High liquidity = many buyers and sellers, fast trades. Low liquidity = you might struggle to find a buyer.

data.question: NSE handles more daily trading volume than BSE. What does 'liquidity' mean in this context?

options.text: The exchange has more cash reserves
How easy it is to buy or sell quickly without the price moving too much
The number of companies listed on the exchange
How often the exchange is open for trading

data.content: Now, who makes sure nobody cheats in this giant marketplace? Enter SEBI -- the Securities and Exchange Board of India. Think of SEBI as the referee. It makes the rules, investigates fraud, and protects investors like you and me. Just like RBI watches over banks, SEBI watches over the stock market.

Without SEBI, stock markets would be the Wild West -- insider trading everywhere, companies faking their numbers, brokers running off with your money. SEBI is the reason you can trust that the game is (mostly) fair.

data.term: SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India)
data.definition: India's stock market regulator, established in 1988. SEBI makes the rules, investigates fraud, and protects investors. Like RBI for banks, SEBI is the watchdog for markets.

data.alt: SEBI as a referee overseeing the stock market game
data.prompt: A bold flat illustration of a referee character wearing a SEBI badge, standing between two stock exchange buildings (BSE and NSE), blowing a whistle. Green (#2ECC71) uniform and accents. Playful but authoritative, filling the frame.

data.question: What is SEBI's role in the Indian stock market?

options.text: It decides which stocks investors should buy
It runs the BSE and NSE directly
It regulates markets, protects investors, and investigates fraud

data.content: One more thing you should know: stock markets in India are open weekdays only, from 9:15 AM to 3:30 PM. Saturdays, Sundays, and public holidays? Closed. Your stocks don't vanish though -- they just sit there in your account, chilling till Monday.

lessons.title: How Stock Prices Move
lessons.subtitle: Supply, demand, and the human heart

data.content: Exam season at any college canteen. Five hundred stressed-out students all want samosas at the same time. The canteen has maybe 200. What happens to the price? It goes up, obviously. More people want them, supply can't keep up, and the canteen uncle starts charging ₹15 instead of ₹10.
Stock prices work on the exact same logic. No different from samosas.

data.alt: A canteen with students lining up for samosas showing supply and demand
data.prompt: A college canteen scene with a long queue of Indian students waiting for samosas. A price board shows the samosa price going up with an arrow. Green (#2ECC71) color palette, bold flat illustration, playful and energetic, filling the frame.

data.content: Every second the market is open, thousands of people are placing buy and sell orders. More people want to buy Infosys than sell it? Price goes up. More people dumping Infosys than buying? Price drops. That's literally it. Supply and demand.

data.definition: The fundamental force that sets prices. More buyers than sellers = price goes up. More sellers than buyers = price goes down. Applies to everything from onions to Infosys shares.

data.question: What happens when demand for a stock exceeds supply (more buyers than sellers)?

options.text: Price drops because sellers are confident
Price rises because buyers compete with each other
Price stays the same because SEBI controls it

data.text: Okay I get supply and demand. But kya farak padta hai what triggers it? Like, why do people suddenly decide to buy or sell a stock on a random Tuesday?

data.content: The biggest trigger is company earnings. Every quarter (3 months), listed companies announce their results -- revenue, profit, growth rate. If Reliance beats expectations, investors get excited and rush to buy. Price climbs. If results disappoint? Sellers flood in and the price sinks.

In March 2020, when Covid lockdowns were announced, Sensex fell from around 41,000 to roughly 25,600 in just 40 days -- a crash of 38%. But here's the twist: by December 2020, just 9 months later, it had bounced back to 47,000. Patience literally paid.

data.question: A company announces quarterly profits that beat analyst expectations. What is the most likely immediate effect on its stock price?

options.text: Price drops because higher profits mean higher taxes
Price stays flat because earnings are already priced in
Price rises because more investors want to buy on the good news

data.alt: News headlines affecting stock prices with arrows showing price going up and down
data.prompt: A split scene: left side shows a positive newspaper headline ('Record Profits!') with a green arrow pointing up, right side shows a negative headline ('CEO Resigns') with a red arrow pointing down. Stock chart in background. Green (#2ECC71) palette for positive side, bold flat style, filling the frame.

data.content: News and events are the second big mover. New product launch, CEO change, government policy shift, competitor gaining ground, RBI hiking interest rates, oil prices spiking -- all of these shake stock prices. The day India announced its first Covid lockdown, Sensex fell 3,935 points. That was the biggest single-day fall ever at the time.

data.definition: The overall mood of investors -- whether optimistic (bullish) or pessimistic (bearish). Sentiment can push prices away from a company's real value in the short term. Think of it as the market's 'mood swings.'

data.content: And then there's the tricky one: investor sentiment. Sometimes prices move not because of any actual news, but because people collectively feel optimistic or scared. Fear and greed are real forces. When everyone panics, they sell even strong companies. When everyone's euphoric, they buy garbage.

Short term, the stock market is basically a popularity contest. Long term, it's a reality check. Warren Buffett nailed it: 'In the short run, the market is a voting machine. In the long run, it's a weighing machine.' Remember that line -- it'll save you money someday.

data.alt: A voting machine on one side and a weighing scale on the other representing short-term vs long-term markets
data.prompt: Left side: a ballot box labeled 'Short Term' with emotional faces (happy, scared) voting. Right side: a weighing scale labeled 'Long Term' with company buildings and profit charts on it. Green (#2ECC71) palette, bold flat illustration, clean split composition.

data.question: Sensex fell 38% in 40 days during March 2020. By December 2020, what had happened?

options.text: It kept falling and took 5 years to recover
It recovered fully and hit new highs around 47,000
SEBI shut down trading until the crisis was over

data.content: Now here's a safety net you should know about: circuit breakers. If a stock falls or rises too fast in a single day, the exchange automatically pauses trading on it. Think of it like speed bumps on a highway. A stock down 20% in one day hits its 'lower circuit' -- trading freezes. Up 20%? 'Upper circuit.' It forces everyone to breathe before making rash decisions.

data.definition: A SEBI-mandated pause in trading when a stock price moves too far too fast. Lower circuit = stock fell by its limit. Upper circuit = stock rose by its limit. Exists to prevent panic-driven crashes.

data.question: A stock has hit its 'upper circuit' for the day. What does this mean?

options.text: The company has reached its maximum market cap
The stock has risen by its maximum allowed limit and trading is paused
The stock can only be sold, not bought
The company is about to be delisted from the exchange

data.text: Circuit breakers are like speed bumps on a highway, yaar. They don't stop the car permanently -- they just force everyone to chill and think before doing something stupid.

data.content: Short-term price movement is noisy and unpredictable. Long-term price movement follows how the actual business performs. The biggest mistake new investors make? Obsessing over daily price changes while ignoring whether the company is actually any good.

exercises.prompt: A stock hits its 'lower circuit' during trading. What does this mean?

exercises.explanation: Positive news (profits, contracts, growth) drives demand and prices up. Negative news (leadership problems, competition, regulation) drives sellers in and prices down. Not always, markets are complex, but these are the dominant tendencies.

exercises.prompt: Stock prices are entirely random and cannot be influenced by company performance.
exercises.explanation: Short-term price moves can seem random, but over the long term, stock prices track company performance closely. A company that grows profits year after year will almost certainly have a higher stock price years later. Short-term = noisy. Long-term = follows fundamentals.

exercises.prompt: Warren Buffett said: 'In the short run, the market is a voting machine. In the long run, it's a weighing machine.' What does 'weighing machine' refer to?

options.text: The weight of the stock certificates

exercises.explanation: Buffett means: in the short term, stocks move based on popularity/sentiment (voting). In the long term, they move based on actual business value, profits, revenue growth, competitive strength (weighing). That's why long-term investors focus on the business, not the daily price.

lessons.title: Sensex & Nifty: The Scoreboard
lessons.subtitle: Reading the economy's daily report card

data.content: Imagine you want to know how India's cricket team is doing, but instead of one scoreboard, you have to check the individual scores of 5,000 players at once. Chaos, right? That's the problem stock market indices solve.
Instead of tracking every single listed company, you track a select group of the biggest, most important ones. Their combined movement tells you how the overall market -- and the economy -- is doing.

data.alt: A cricket scoreboard transforming into a stock market index display
data.prompt: A cricket scoreboard on the left with player scores, an arrow in the middle, and a stock market index display on the right showing 'Sensex: 75,000' and 'Nifty: 22,000'. Green (#2ECC71) palette, bold flat style, playful comparison layout, filling the frame.

data.content: Meet the Sensex and the Nifty 50 -- India's two headline-making market indices. Every news broadcast, every business newspaper, every uncle's WhatsApp forward about the economy mentions at least one. After this lesson, you'll actually know what those numbers mean.

data.definition: A carefully selected basket of stocks used to represent the overall performance of the market. Like an average, but smarter -- weighted by the size of each company.

data.question: What problem does a stock market index like the Sensex solve?

options.text: It sets the price of individual stocks each day
It tracks a select group of top companies so you can gauge overall market performance
It prevents stocks from falling below a minimum price

data.text: My dad keeps saying 'Sensex hit 75,000 today' like it's some huge deal. What does that number even mean? Is 75,000 good?

It means the combined value of India's top 30 companies is 750 times what it was in 1979 when Sensex started at 100. But honestly, the number alone doesn't say much. What matters is the change -- like 'up 500 points' or 'down 1.2%.'

data.content: The Sensex (short for Sensitive Index) tracks 30 of the biggest, most actively traded companies on BSE. India's economic dream team: Reliance, TCS, HDFC Bank, Infosys, ITC, Bajaj Finance. It started at a base value of 100 in 1979. In 2024, it crossed 75,000. That means these 30 companies, as a group, are worth 750x what they were 45 years ago.

data.definition: BSE's benchmark index tracking 30 of India's biggest companies. Base value: 100 in 1979. As of 2024, trading around 72,000 to 75,000. Weighted by each company's market cap, so the biggest companies influence the index more.

data.content: If someone had invested ₹1 lakh in a Sensex index fund in 1979, it would be worth roughly ₹7.5 crore today. No stock picking, no timing the market. Just parking money and waiting for 45 years. That's the power of long-term compounding.

data.alt: Chart showing Sensex growth from 100 in 1979 to 75,000 in 2024
data.prompt: A line chart with x-axis from 1979 to 2024, y-axis showing Sensex value. Line goes from 100 to 75,000 with marked dips at 2008 and 2020 crashes, then recovery. Annotation: 'Every crash was followed by a new high'. Green (#2ECC71) line, bold flat style, clean data visualization.

data.question: How many companies does the Sensex track, and on which exchange?

options.text: 50 companies on NSE
30 companies on BSE
100 companies on both BSE and NSE
30 companies on NSE

data.content: The Nifty 50 (short for National Fifty) tracks the 50 largest companies on NSE. It's broader than the Sensex -- 50 companies across 13 sectors instead of 30 -- so it captures a wider slice of India's economy. Nifty's base value was 1,000 in November 1995. In 2024, it's around 21,000 to 22,000. That's a 21-22x increase in roughly 29 years.

data.definition: NSE's benchmark index tracking 50 of India's biggest companies across 13 sectors. Base value: 1,000 in November 1995. As of 2024, trading around 21,000 to 22,000. The most widely used benchmark for measuring stock market performance in India.

data.content: Stop freaking out about '500 point falls.' Always look at the percentage change, not the absolute number. A 500-point fall when Sensex is at 75,000 is just 0.67%. Your chai costs fluctuate more than that when the doodh-wala changes prices.

data.alt: Comparison showing 500 points means different things at different Sensex levels
data.prompt: Two scenarios side by side. Left: Sensex at 3,000 with a 500 point fall labeled '16.7% CRASH'. Right: Sensex at 75,000 with a 500 point fall labeled '0.67% blip'. Shocked face on left, calm face on right. Green (#2ECC71) palette, bold flat style, filling the frame.

data.question: The Sensex falls 1,000 points when it is at 75,000. What percentage drop is this?

options.text: About 1.33%
About 7.5%

data.content: Both Sensex and Nifty are market-cap weighted. This means the bigger the company, the more it influences the index. Reliance, TCS, and HDFC Bank are so massive that when they move, the entire index moves with them. When these giants sneeze, the Sensex catches a cold.

data.definition: An index where each company's influence is proportional to its market cap. A ₹10 lakh crore company moves the index more than a ₹1 lakh crore company, even if both go up by the same percentage.

data.question: In a market-cap weighted index, which company has more influence on the index value?

options.text: Every company has equal influence regardless of size
The company with the highest market cap has the most influence
The company with the highest share price has the most influence
The newest company added to the index

data.content: When you invest in a Nifty 50 index fund, you automatically buy tiny pieces of all 50 companies in proportion to their size. It's one of the simplest and most effective investment strategies out there -- but that's a story for Chapter 2.

exercises.prompt: The Sensex started at a base value of 100 in 1979. If it's now at 75,000, what does this tell you?

options.text: There are 750 more companies listed today than in 1979
The combined value of the top 30 BSE companies is 750 times what it was in 1979
The Indian rupee has inflated 750 times since 1979
Each of the 30 companies has grown exactly 750 times

exercises.explanation: The index value reflects the collective market cap movement of its constituent stocks. Sensex at 75,000 vs base 100 means the basket of 30 stocks is collectively worth 750 times their 1979 value. Not each company individually, the average across all 30.

exercises.scenario: You're watching the news. The anchor says: 'Sensex fell 2,000 points today, the biggest single-day fall this year!' Your parent looks worried. But Sensex is currently at 78,000.
exercises.prompt: How should you interpret this 2,000-point fall?

options.text: It's catastrophic, 2,000 points is huge
It's a 2.56% fall, significant but not unusual or catastrophic
It means the economy has shrunk by 2,000
All 30 Sensex companies lost exactly 2,000 points each

exercises.explanation: 2,000 ÷ 78,000 = 2.56%. That's a notable single-day fall (markets usually move 0.5–1% daily), but it's not catastrophic. Headlines love big absolute numbers because they sound scary. Always convert to percentage to get the real picture.

exercises.prompt: How many companies does the Nifty 50 track?
exercises.explanation: Nifty 50 tracks 50 companies listed on NSE. The Sensex (BSE) tracks 30. The Nifty 100 and Nifty 500 are broader indices, but Nifty 50 is the most widely used benchmark in India.

exercises.prompt: In a market-cap weighted index, all companies have equal influence on the index movement.
exercises.explanation: Market-cap weighted means bigger companies (Reliance, TCS, HDFC Bank) have much more influence than smaller ones. If Reliance rises 2% and a smaller company falls 2%, the index will likely be up, because Reliance's total value impact is far larger.

exercises.prompt: What was the Nifty 50's base value when it was launched in 1995?
exercises.explanation: Nifty 50 started with a base value of 1,000 in November 1995. Today it's around 21,000–22,000, representing roughly a 21x growth. This includes dividends and compounding over ~29 years.

lessons.title: How to Actually Buy Stocks
lessons.subtitle: Demat accounts and your first trade

data.content: So you've decided you want to buy Infosys stock. You've read up, you're convinced. Now what? You can't exactly walk into a shop and say 'bhaiya, 5 Infosys de do.' But the real process is surprisingly simple -- and in India today, anyone with a phone and ₹100 can start.

data.alt: A teen looking at a smartphone showing a stock trading app
data.prompt: An Indian teen holding a smartphone with a stock trading app on screen showing Infosys stock with a green Buy button. Clean phone UI visible. Green (#2ECC71) palette, bold flat illustration, modern and relatable, filling the frame.

data.content: You need two things: a Demat account and a Trading account. Your Demat account is your digital locker -- it stores your shares electronically, like a bank account stores money. Your Trading account is the interface where you actually place buy and sell orders. Most brokers bundle both together when you sign up.

data.definition: A digital account that holds your shares electronically. Just like a bank account holds your money, a Demat account holds your stocks. Maintained by depositories: NSDL (for NSE) and CDSL (for BSE).

data.content: Before 1996, shares were actual paper certificates. You'd get a literal piece of paper saying 'You own 50 shares of Tata Steel.' People lost lakhs when certificates got damaged, stolen, or eaten by termites. India went fully digital in 1996. Now your holdings are just entries in a database -- no termite risk.

data.question: What are the two accounts you need to trade stocks in India?

options.text: Savings account and current account
Demat account and trading account
PAN account and Aadhaar account

data.text: Wait, people used to carry around paper certificates for their stocks?! What if you lost them?

Exactly yaar! People literally lost lakhs because a piece of paper got damaged. That's why India moved everything digital. Now your shares sit safely in your Demat account -- same vibe as money sitting in your Google Pay.

data.content: India's major brokers: Zerodha (largest by active clients, started by Nithin Kamath in Bengaluru), Groww (super popular with first-time young investors), Upstox (backed by Ratan Tata), Angel One, and ICICI Direct. Zerodha and Groww are discount brokers -- they charge ₹0 to ₹20 per trade. Banks like ICICI or HDFC also offer trading but charge more.

data.definition: A company that executes your buy and sell orders on the exchange. They make money by charging a brokerage fee per trade. In India: Zerodha, Groww, Upstox, Angel One, ICICI Direct.

data.question: Before 1996, how were shares held in India?

options.text: In digital Demat accounts, same as today
As physical paper certificates
Shares didn't exist before 1996
Through UPI-based wallets

data.alt: Step-by-step flow showing how to buy your first stock in India
data.prompt: A vertical numbered flow diagram with 5 steps: (1) Choose a broker app with Zerodha/Groww icons, (2) Complete KYC with PAN card and Aadhaar icons, (3) Fund your trading account with rupee symbol, (4) Search for stock with magnifying glass, (5) Place buy order with green button. Green (#2ECC71) step numbers, bold flat style, clean layout.

data.content: To open a Demat account, you need: PAN card (mandatory), Aadhaar for KYC verification (proving your identity), a bank account for fund transfers, and you must be at least 18 (minors can have accounts under a parent's guardianship). The entire process is online now and takes 15-30 minutes. Account opening is free on most platforms.

Pro tip for beginners: always double-check the quantity before tapping 'Buy.' Legend has it, a trader once meant to buy 1 share of a ₹5,000 stock and accidentally ordered 1,000 shares -- blowing ₹50 lakh in one fat-finger moment. Most apps have confirmation screens now. Still, check twice.

Once your account is funded, you place orders. Two main types. A market order says 'buy this right now at whatever price it's at.' A limit order says 'buy this only if the price drops to ₹X or below.' Market orders execute instantly. Limit orders wait -- and expire at end of day if unfilled.

data.definition: Market order: buy/sell immediately at current price. Limit order: buy/sell only when price hits a level you specify. Market = speed. Limit = control over price.

data.question: You want to buy a stock, but only if it drops to ₹500 or below. It is currently at ₹540. Which order type should you use?

options.text: Market order, to buy immediately at ₹540
Limit order set at ₹500
You cannot specify a price; the exchange decides

data.alt: Comparison of market order (instant purchase) vs limit order (conditional purchase)
data.prompt: Split scene. Left side: a person pressing a big green 'BUY NOW' button, stock purchased instantly, labeled 'Market Order'. Right side: a person setting a target price on a dial, waiting patiently, labeled 'Limit Order'. Green (#2ECC71) palette, bold flat style, clear comparison layout.

data.content: When you sell a stock for a profit, the taxman comes knocking. If you held the stock for less than 1 year, you pay Short-Term Capital Gains (STCG) tax at 20%. If you held for more than 1 year, you pay Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) tax at 12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh per year. Holding longer = paying less tax. Something to keep in mind before you sell.

data.definition: Tax on profits from selling stocks. STCG (held under 1 year): 20%. LTCG (held over 1 year): 12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh/year. Rates as of Budget 2024.

data.question: You bought a stock for ₹5,000 and sold it 14 months later for ₹7,000. Which tax rate applies to your ₹2,000 profit?

options.text: STCG at 20%, because all stock profits are short-term
LTCG at 12.5%, because you held for more than 1 year
No tax applies on stock market gains in India
GST at 18%

data.content: You don't need big money to start. Groww and Zerodha let you buy as little as 1 share. If TCS is at ₹3,800, you can buy exactly 1 share for ₹3,800. There's no minimum beyond that. Your first trade can be smaller than your monthly phone recharge.

data.alt: A small plant growing from a single coin representing starting small with investing
data.prompt: A small green plant sprouting from a single rupee coin, growing into a tree with stock certificates as leaves. A teen watering it with a small watering can. Green (#2ECC71) palette, bold flat illustration, hopeful and motivating, filling the frame.

exercises.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a Demat account?

options.text: To store cash for investing
To hold your shares electronically in digital form
To transfer money between banks
To file income tax returns

exercises.explanation: A Demat (Dematerialised) account stores your shares electronically, think of it as a bank account but for stocks instead of money. It replaced physical share certificates after 1996.

exercises.scenario: Arjun wants to buy Wipro shares. He thinks Wipro is currently overpriced at ₹480 and wants to buy only if the price dips to ₹450 or below. His friend tells him to just place a market order right now.
exercises.prompt: Which order type should Arjun use, and why?

options.text: Market order, to buy immediately at ₹480
Limit order at ₹450, so he only buys if the price hits his target
Limit order at ₹480, same as market order in this case
He can't buy at a specific price, markets don't work that way

exercises.explanation: Arjun wants price control, he'll buy at ₹450, not ₹480. That's a textbook limit order. If Wipro never drops to ₹450 before market close, his order stays unfilled (and he doesn't buy). Market orders would execute at ₹480 immediately, not what Arjun wants.

exercises.prompt: Sort these items into what you DO and DON'T need to open a Demat account in India
exercises.explanation: You need PAN, Aadhaar (for KYC), a bank account, and a broker. There's no minimum deposit, you can fund as little as you want. Physical certificates are ancient history, shares are electronic since 1996.

exercises.prompt: In India, a market order to buy stocks will be executed immediately at the current trading price.
exercises.explanation: A market order says 'buy at whatever price is available right now.' During market hours, it executes almost instantly. The slight risk is that by the time the order goes through, the price may have moved a few paise, this is called 'slippage,' and it's negligible for most regular investors.

exercises.prompt: You bought a stock for ₹10,000 and sold it 8 months later for ₹13,000. What type of tax applies on your ₹3,000 profit?

options.text: Long-term capital gains tax (LTCG) at 12.5%
Short-term capital gains tax (STCG) at 20%
No tax, equity gains are tax-free
GST at 18%

exercises.explanation: You held for 8 months (less than 12 months), so STCG applies at 20%. Tax = 20% × ₹3,000 = ₹600. Had you held for more than 12 months, LTCG of 12.5% would apply (on gains above ₹1.25 lakh threshold). Holding longer is usually more tax-efficient.

lessons.title: Bulls, Bears & Market Moods
lessons.subtitle: When the market is on fire, and when it's in the freezer

data.content: It's 2021. You open Zerodha and everything is green. Your portfolio is up. Your random IPO applications are getting allotted. Your friend who never cared about stocks is now sending you stock tips on WhatsApp. That uncle who always called the stock market 'gambling'? Yeah, he quietly opened a demat account last week.
That vibe, that energy where everything keeps going up and everyone's a genius? That's a bull market.

data.alt: A charging bull surrounded by green stock charts going up
data.prompt: A powerful bull charging forward through rising green stock charts. Confetti and green arrows everywhere. Indian teens in the background celebrating with phones showing green portfolios. Green (#2ECC71) palette, bold flat illustration, energetic and dynamic, filling the frame.

data.content: Now flip the scene. March 2020. Covid just hit. Markets have crashed 38% in 40 days. Every headline is terrifying. Your portfolio looks like a horror movie. That uncle? He's deleted the Zerodha app. Everyone is convinced it's only going to get worse. That's a bear market.

data.definition: A market condition where stock prices are rising, investor confidence is high, and optimism reigns. Technically defined as a 20%+ rise from a recent low, sustained over months. The bull 'charges up' -- hence the name.

data.text: Why bulls and bears though? That's such a random pair of animals yaar.
Nah it actually makes sense! A bull attacks by thrusting its horns upward -- like rising prices. A bear swipes its paws downward -- like falling prices. Once you picture it, you'll never forget.

data.definition: A market condition where stock prices are falling, investor confidence is low, and pessimism spreads. Technically defined as a 20%+ drop from a recent high. The bear 'swipes down' -- hence the name.

data.question: A bull attacks by thrusting its horns upward. In stock market terms, a 'bull market' means:

options.text: Prices are falling sharply and investors are fearful
Prices are rising, confidence is high, and optimism reigns
Trading volume is extremely low

data.content: The famous Wall Street charging bull statue in New York weighs 3,200 kilograms and was originally guerrilla art -- someone just left it there in 1989. It became the worldwide symbol of bullish markets. BSE has its own bull statue outside its building on Dalal Street!

data.alt: A bear swiping down at falling stock charts in a gloomy market scene
data.prompt: A large bear swiping downward at falling red stock charts. Dark clouds overhead. People looking worried at their phones. Contrast with muted tones but green (#2ECC71) accent on a small 'This too shall pass' sign. Bold flat illustration, dramatic composition, filling the frame.

data.content: Here's the pattern in Indian markets: 2003-2008 was a massive bull run -- Sensex went from 3,000 to 21,000. Then the 2008 global financial crisis triggered a brutal bear market, crashing Sensex to around 8,000 by early 2009. Then another bull run. Covid crash in 2020 (-38%). Each time: full recovery and new highs within 1-3 years.

Bear markets are just the stock market running a clearance sale. When solid companies get cheaper because everyone's panicking, that's actually when smart investors load up. Buffett's famous line: 'Be fearful when others are greedy, and greedy when others are fearful.' Tattoo that on your brain.

data.question: In March 2020, the Sensex crashed 38% due to Covid. By December 2020, what had happened?

options.text: It had fallen another 20% and kept declining
It recovered fully and continued to new highs around 47,000
It stayed flat at the crash level for years
SEBI suspended trading until 2021

data.content: The dangerous thing about bear markets isn't the falling prices. It's your brain. Every cell in your body screams 'SELL EVERYTHING' when headlines are terrifying and your portfolio is red. This panic-selling is how most regular investors lock in their losses. The people who stayed invested through 2020's crash? They watched their portfolios hit all-time highs by early 2021.

data.alt: Sensex chart showing bull and bear phases from 2000 to 2024 with annotations
data.prompt: A line chart of Sensex from 2000 to 2024. Green shaded bull phases and grey shaded bear phases. Labels: '2008 Crisis -60%', 'Covid 2020 -38%', '2003-2007 Bull +800%', '2020-2021 Recovery'. Overall upward trend despite dips. Green (#2ECC71) for bull phases, bold flat data viz style.

data.question: During a bear market, most retail investors panic and sell at the bottom. What typically happens to the market after a bear phase?

options.text: It never recovers; those losses are permanent
It eventually recovers and often reaches new highs
Only foreign investors can buy during recovery

data.content: One more important term: a market correction. This is a drop of 10-20% from a recent peak. Corrections are healthy, normal, and happen every 1-2 years on average. A correction is NOT a crash. It's the market stretching its legs before climbing again. Don't confuse it with a bear market (20%+ sustained fall).

data.definition: A decline of 10 to 20% in stock prices from a recent high. Normal and healthy, happens roughly every 1 to 2 years. Not a crash, not a bear market. Just the market taking a breather.

data.question: Ravi's portfolio dropped 12% from its peak. His friend says it is a 'market correction.' Is his friend right?

options.text: No, any drop is a full bear market
Yes, a 10-20% drop from a recent high is called a correction, which is normal
No, corrections only happen once every decade

data.content: Don't confuse a bull market with skill. When everything is rising, even random stock picks look genius. This is when new investors start believing they can't lose. Then the bear arrives and the illusion shatters. True investing skill shows in how you handle the bears, not the bulls.

data.alt: A person calmly investing while others panic during a market dip
data.prompt: Split scene: on the left, panicked investors selling and running away from falling charts. On the right, one calm Indian teen sitting peacefully, buying stocks on their phone with a small smile. Green (#2ECC71) palette, bold flat style, clear contrast between panic and calm, filling the frame.

exercises.prompt: What is the technical definition of a bear market?

options.text: Any day the market closes in the red
A fall of more than 5% in a single week
A sustained drop of 20% or more from a recent high
When trading volume falls below 50% of the average

exercises.explanation: A bear market is technically defined as a 20%+ fall from a recent peak, sustained over time (not a single-day crash). A single bad day is just a bad day. A 10–20% fall is a correction. 20%+ sustained fall = bear market.

exercises.scenario: Meera invested ₹50,000 in a diversified set of Nifty 50 stocks in February 2020. By March 2020 (just 5 weeks later), her portfolio was worth only ₹31,000, a 38% loss. Everyone around her was selling. She chose to hold and even invested another ₹20,000 in April 2020.
exercises.prompt: By December 2020, the market had fully recovered to pre-Covid levels and continued rising. What does Meera's strategy illustrate?

options.text: Lucky timing, she shouldn't have held during such a big crash
That holding through bear markets and investing during dips can lead to strong long-term returns
That individual stocks are better than diversified portfolios
That bear markets always recover within 5 weeks

exercises.explanation: Meera used the bear market correctly: she didn't panic-sell at a 38% loss. She held, and even bought more at depressed prices. By year end, her original ₹50,000 was back to ₹50,000+ AND her ₹20,000 April investment had appreciated significantly. This is exactly what Buffett means by 'being greedy when others are fearful.'

exercises.prompt: Sort these into Bull Market Signals vs Bear Market Signals

items.text: Record demat account openings, everyone wants to invest
Foreign investors pulling billions out of Indian markets
GDP growth accelerating, RBI cutting interest rates
Every news article predicts further market decline

exercises.explanation: Bull markets are characterized by optimism, investment inflows, strong economic signals, and high IPO demand. Bear markets show the opposite, fear, selling, weak fundamentals, negative sentiment. Both are normal parts of the cycle.

exercises.prompt: A market correction (10-20% drop) is a rare, once-in-a-decade event in Indian markets.
exercises.explanation: Market corrections (10–20% drops) happen roughly every 1–2 years on average. They're completely normal. In any given decade, Indian markets have had multiple corrections. What's rare is a full bear market (20%+ sustained fall), those are less frequent but also always eventually recovered.

exercises.prompt: Warren Buffett said: 'Be fearful when others are greedy, and greedy when others are fearful.' In terms of market cycles, what does 'greedy when others are fearful' mean?

options.text: Buy aggressively when markets are at all-time highs and everyone is excited
Buy when markets are falling and most investors are panicking and selling
Sell everything when prices drop even slightly
Only invest in safe assets like gold during market downturns

exercises.explanation: Buffett's go-against-the-crowd wisdom: when everyone's panicking (fearful) and selling, prices drop to attractive levels, that's when quality stocks are 'on sale.' Being 'greedy' means buying during these fearful moments, not selling. This requires emotional discipline, which is harder than it sounds.

simulation.title: Trader for a Day
simulation.description: You've just been given access to a virtual trading account with ₹10,000. It's 9:15 AM. Five stocks are live on your screen. The market closes at 3:30 PM. News will break throughout the day. Every decision matters.

nodes.narrative: The opening bell rings. Your screen shows five stocks, all flashing green from yesterday's positive session. You have ₹10,000 and the whole day ahead of you. The first rule of trading: don't rush. But also, don't just sit there. Your friend Aryan has already bought Zomato. Your cousin says Reliance is 'definitely going to 3,000 today.' What do you do?

choices.text: Buy 5 shares of Reliance at ₹2,850 (costs ₹14,250), wait, you only have ₹10,000. Focus on what you can afford.
choices.feedback: Chip raises an eyebrow. 'Infosys? Solid, well-established IT company. Risky that you put 88% of your capital in one stock though. Hope nothing weird happens in IT today...'

choices.text: Split: Buy 3 shares of Zomato (₹585) + 1 share of HDFC Bank (₹1,620), spread it out
choices.feedback: Chip nods approvingly. 'Diversification on day one! Banking and food tech, different sectors. If one goes down, the other might hold. Now you have ₹7,795 left to deploy later.'

choices.text: Hold, don't buy anything yet. Watch the market for the first 30 minutes
choices.feedback: Chip gives a little golf clap. 'The first 15-30 minutes after open are often the most volatile. Experienced traders call this the 'noise window.' Watching first is smart.'

nodes.narrative: BREAKING: The US Federal Reserve hints at more interest rate hikes. Global IT stocks are dipping. Infosys (INFY) is down 2.3% from your buy price of ₹1,480, now at ₹1,446. choices.text: Sell Infosys at ₹1,446, cut your losses before it falls more
choices.feedback: Chip sighs. 'You panic-sold on a 2.3% dip. That's called getting spooked by short-term noise. Infosys is a fundamentally strong company. A Fed announcement dip is usually temporary in quality IT stocks. Let's see how this plays out.'

choices.text: Hold Infosys AND use remaining ₹600 to buy 3 more shares of Zomato at ₹195
choices.feedback: Chip approves the Zomato addition. 'But Infosys is bleeding right now. You're holding a paper loss of ₹204, meaning the value has dropped but you haven't actually sold, so you haven't locked in the loss yet. Can you stomach watching it fall more before (hopefully) recovering?'

choices.text: Use ₹600 to buy Tata Motors, 0 shares (price is ₹910, you can't afford 1 share with ₹600)
choices.feedback: Chip smirks. 'Can't buy 0.66 of a share, friend. You'd need ₹910 to buy even 1 Tata Motors share. This is why spreading your capital matters, you don't want to get stuck with too little to act on new opportunities.'

nodes.narrative: Good news: Zomato just announced record quarterly orders, 'highest ever total order value.' Zomato is now ₹208 (up 6.6% from your buy price of ₹195). Your 3 shares show a ₹39 gain. HDFC Bank is flat. You still have ₹7,795 in cash. Tata Motors is rallying on EV contract news, up 4% to ₹946.

choices.text: Buy 8 more shares of Zomato at ₹208 (₹1,664), ride the momentum
choices.feedback: Chip looks nervous. 'Chasing a stock after it's already up 6.6% today is called buying the momentum. Sometimes it works. Sometimes you're the last buyer before it reverses. Watch this carefully.'

choices.text: Buy 6 shares of Tata Motors at ₹946 (₹5,676), EV news is a real catalyst
choices.feedback: Chip nods. 'Tata Motors winning EV contracts is a genuine business catalyst. You're buying on news, but at least it's real news with real impact. The EV sector has strong tailwinds in India.'

choices.text: Hold cash, watch and wait, it's still early
choices.feedback: Chip gives you a knowing look. 'Patience. You have ₹7,795 to deploy intelligently. What's the rush? Good opportunities will present themselves.'

nodes.timeLabel: 10:30 AM - You Waited. Here's What Happened.
nodes.narrative: Smart move. The first 30 minutes were wild. Zomato jumped 7% on order volume news, then pulled back to just 4% up. Infosys dipped 2% on US rate hike fears, then stabilized. Tata Motors is up 4% on an EV contract win and holding steady. Now the picture is clearer. You have all ₹10,000 and better information than people who rushed at open.

choices.text: Buy 5 shares of Tata Motors at ₹946 (₹4,730), EV is the future, solid catalyst
choices.feedback: Chip approves. 'You waited for clarity, then bought on a real business development. That's how patient investors operate. Now you have ₹5,270 in reserve, plenty for the afternoon.'

choices.text: Buy a mix: 3 shares HDFC Bank (₹4,860) + 10 shares Zomato (₹2,020)
choices.feedback: Chip nods. 'Nice diversification. Banking (stable, fundamental) + food tech (growth, volatile). Two very different risk profiles. This is how a thoughtful portfolio gets built.'

choices.text: Buy 6 shares of Infosys at ₹1,450 (₹8,700), it dipped on the Fed news but it's a strong company -- buy the dip
choices.feedback: Chip raises an eyebrow. 'Buying the dip on a quality company -- bold move. Infosys is solid long-term, and a 2% dip on Fed noise could be a gift. But you've put 87% in one stock. Concentrated bets cut both ways.'

nodes.timeLabel: 1:00 PM - You Sold. Here's What Happened.
nodes.narrative: You sold Infosys at ₹1,446, taking a ₹204 loss. And then... Infosys recovered. By 1 PM, it's back at ₹1,465 and climbing. The Fed rate hike concern turned out to be overblown. Infosys had dipped, not fallen. You have ₹9,072 in cash now. The afternoon session begins. Tata Motors is still holding its gains at ₹952.

choices.text: Buy back into Infosys now at ₹1,465 (buy 6 shares for ₹8,790)

choices.text: Move on, buy 4 shares of Tata Motors at ₹952 (₹3,808) and hold cash
choices.feedback: Chip thinks. 'Reasonable pivot. You took a small loss on Infosys but you're repositioning around a stronger catalyst. Cut losses, find the next opportunity.'

Then: a rumour starts circulating that a major food delivery app is about to launch in India and directly compete with Zomato.

content.scenario: A new food-tech startup IPO is live, they make software for restaurant billing. Your college friend says 'Everyone is applying, it'll list at 60% premium for sure!' The IPO is priced at ₹450/share. The company has never made a profit and has been operating for only 2 years.
content.prompt: What's the smartest approach to this IPO?

options.text: Apply for maximum shares, 60% listing gain is too good to miss
Skip it entirely, all IPOs are bad
Research the company's fundamentals and IPO documents before deciding, don't invest just on FOMO
Apply for a small amount so you limit your downside but catch the upside

content.explanation: IPO hype is real but often wrong. Zomato listed at +52% in 2021. Paytm IPO in 2021 listed at -27% on day one and fell further for months. A 2-year-old, unprofitable company at ₹450/share deserves serious scrutiny before you put money in. The right answer is always: read the company's IPO document (called the prospectus), understand how the business makes money and whether it's growing, then decide. Never invest on a friend's tip alone.

content.scenario: You bought ₹20,000 of Nifty 50 index fund 6 months ago. Today, bad global news has sent markets crashing, your portfolio is now showing ₹16,400 (an 18% loss). Your dad says 'Sell everything before it falls more.' Your mum says 'Hold and don't look at it.'
content.prompt: What does good long-term investing wisdom say?

options.text: Sell immediately, 18% loss is too painful, protect what's left
Hold and consider investing more if possible, corrections are normal and index funds recover
Sell half, keep half, compromise between safety and long-term growth
Switch to gold, it always goes up when markets fall

content.explanation: An 18% fall in a diversified index fund (not a single stock) is a market correction, not a catastrophe. The Nifty 50 has recovered from every single correction in its history. Selling at the bottom locks in your loss. Holding (and ideally buying more) is what long-term wealth is built on. The Mum strategy ('hold and don't look') is emotionally and statistically sound for index fund investors.

content.prompt: Which of these is the correct sequence of steps to buy your first stock in India?

options.text: Walk to BSE → pay cash → get certificate
Open Demat account → complete KYC → fund account → search stock → place order
Call a broker on the phone → tell them what to buy → they handle the rest
Create a Zerodha account → that's it, you can start buying immediately

content.explanation: The full process: (1) Choose a broker like Zerodha or Groww, (2) Open Demat + Trading account with KYC (PAN + Aadhaar), (3) Fund your trading account from your bank, (4) Search for your stock, (5) Place buy order. The old 'call a broker' system still exists but 99% of retail investors now use apps. KYC completion is mandatory before the first trade.
